data.name: Homefront®: The Revolution
data.detailed_description:
Story


Four years into the brutal military occupation, America is on its knees.

Philadelphia - once the birthplace of Independence - has become a ghetto, where surveillance drones and armoured patrols keep the population at heel, crushing any dissent with savage force.

Her once-proud citizens live in a police state, forced to collaborate just to survive, their dreams of freedom long since extinguished.

But in the badlands of the Red Zone, in the bombed out streets and abandoned subways, a Resistance is forming. A guerrilla force, determined to fight for their freedoms despite overwhelming odds and ignite the second American Revolution.

But Freedom always has a price…

Overview


Homefront®: The Revolution is an open-world first person shooter where you must lead the Resistance movement in guerrilla warfare against a superior military force.

A living, breathing, open world responds to your actions - you and your Resistance Cell can inspire a rebellion on the streets and turn Occupation into Revolution, as oppressed civilians take up the fight.

But your enemy has the advantage - superior technology, firepower, heavy armour and air support. You must learn the art of guerrilla warfare – ambush, sabotage, infiltration, deception – and fight a running battle through the war-ravaged suburbs of Philadelphia.

And the single player campaign is just the start – in Co-Op you and your friends can form your own Resistance Cell and become renowned as Heroes of the Revolution.

Features


• Explore a living, breathing open world - experience true open world gameplay in a first person shooter, brought to life with astonishing CRYENGINE-powered visuals

• Wage Guerrilla Warfare - this is no linear shooter; learn the art of guerrilla warfare and use ambush, infiltration and hit and run tactics against your foe in thrilling un-scripted firefights

• Build the Resistance - recruit revolutionaries to the cause, establish bases and safehouses, capture and customise a deadly arsenal, and build improvised, homebrew weapons for your Guerrilla Tool Kit

• Ignite the Revolution - from oppressed citizen to revolutionary leader, an epic single-player campaign tells the story of the second War of Independence. The dynamic, evolving world responds to your actions as an oppressed nation rises up in defiance against the occupation

• Online Co-Op - take the battle online, form a Resistance Cell with your friends and earn your reputation as Heroes of the Revolution

reviews.review:
For most of the review: https://backloggd.com/u/gamemast15r/review/5510137/

Alright lets address what the most important thing is for this game, which is obviously the gameplay. If I addressed the original Homefront as “TEMU Call of Duty”, this one would be classified as “cheaper Far Cry”, which to be honest I much prefer. It’s a much smaller open world in the sense that you have several different smaller districts that you’ll encounter, each with different bases, stashes and outposts to slowly take over away from the KPA. In some of these districts (i.e. “The Yellow Districts”), you’ll need to slowly convince people to fight back against the oppressors by doing these bases but also completing random encounters such as assassinating KPA officials, destroying KPA drone vehicles, turning on radios and cutting the power to speakers amongst other things as it slowly raises the “Hearts and Minds”, though you can only activate it once you get through further story missions. You’ll commonly encounter KPA patrols and you’re encouraged to sneak around in plain sight and gather around groups of people so that you’re not spotted by the soldiers or by drones who will identify you on sight. As for “The Red Districts”, they’re basically barren wastelands that only really contain resistance members and KPA patrols (which includes a giant blimp that will spot you if you’re under their light, which will cause backup squads to hunt you down on full alert). Since these districts are rather large, you can either travel by front or through various Resistance stashes that hold hidden motorcycles for travel. Taking over some of these outposts and bases will mostly have you do objectives like “Blow up the gas tanks by turning a valve without interruption” or “kill everyone”, rather simple stuff but still alright nonetheless. As you take over bases and slices of territory, resistance members will spawn in, which means if you need backup you can go up to them and tell them to follow you into whatever fight you wish. You also end up unlocking specific tokens and money (though you can also do side jobs) which can be used to buy upgrades, perks, attachments and the like to upgrade your arsenal or your numerous explosive options. 

That’s kind of a general gist on a lot of the extra mechanics in the game, though I do wanna mention my most unrealistic and favorite one: weapon swapping. [spoiler]Not in the sense that you swap weapons, but that you can switch out pieces of your firearms and replace them with others to turn them into different types of guns. Lets use the Assault Rifle as an example. You can change the type of weapon to be an LMG on the fly with an ACOG scope, then change it back to the Assault Rifle with the Holographic, then you can change your Pistol into a Submachine gun by swapping out a part or two. Is it unrealistic? Yeah probably. But I’ll say that it’s actually pretty cool and adds a bit of strategy into the game that I haven’t seen anyone else really use. Say you wanna sweep through a base with a silenced pistol but you get spotted, so the pistol is kind of useless damage wise. Switch it out attachment wise with the submachine gun one and you have a bit more firepower in that moment. Wanna blow up a drone with an explosive but don’t wanna be near it? Switch from regular pipe bombs to the RC Drone Car and ride it up to the back of the drone and blow it up from a distance.[/spoiler] It’s stuff like that I find to be pretty cool. Otherwise I don’t really have too much to say about a lot of the gameplay mechanics that I wouldn’t have said playing Far Cry or any other adjacent game for that matter as it’s a bit more like those games except you’re more susceptible to dying quickly and that it’s a bit less fluid. That being said though, it was actually a really comfortable game and one that I had more often than not enjoyed heavily despite it being rather “unoriginal” than its contemporaries. Like Terminator: Resistance and Sniper Ghost Warrior: Contracts, while my rating for the gameplay would be a 3.5 out of 5, it’s VERY HIGH 3.5 out of 5 compared to the original Homefront’s 3 out of 5 (which was only that way due to it being playable and having some interesting concepts). 

I also wanna state that the game comes with a co-op mode of sorts, but it’s more so you create a character and customize them before you and your friends (or randoms) are thrown out into a district to do missions, but it’s way different from the campaign and I didn’t play it just due to the fact I didn’t really have anyone to play it with so I can’t offer much in the way of critiques. 

Overall I felt that Homefront: The Revolution was the exact kind of game that I wanted to play when I went into it at the moment: the AA Experience akin to Robocop: Rogue City or Terminator: Resistance, but leaning more towards Sniper Ghost Warrior: Contracts in the sense that it’s also more like Far Cry but smaller. The gameplay wasn’t ambitious for certain but it felt nice, visceral, hell even safe but in the most comfy way possible. I know the general feeling for games is that a lot of games shouldn’t play it safe but honestly not every game should be the most groundbreaking brand new experience that you can’t get anywhere else. I enjoyed going through the smaller open world districts, taking over outposts and taking down any Norks that I saw with a variety of explosive options and my trusty Assault Rifle that I transformed into a Light Machine Gun through a highly unrealistic yet greatly satisfying weapon customization system. Graphically I felt the game looked pretty solid and I actually kind of liked the oppressive atmospheric rubble of Philadelphia, as running through makeshift buildings reminded me of Terminator: Resistance followed by the switch to a Deus Ex styled peace and calm. I can’t always say that the story had “moved me” per se, but I’ll definitely say that I understood and cared about the character motivations with this title a lot more considering they had a lot more screen time to flesh everything out and give you a handle on their motivations, and would say that it lives up more to the concept that I felt the previous game had as well. The sound was for the most part pretty good and I can’t really say I had much to say about them other than giving it a solid thumbs up and saying that I really liked how the guns sound. Overall I feel like the game got a lot of bad reviews at the time due to the bugs and glitches, which I completely understand and would say should not be normalized at all even if it sadly is. Post Release however? I’d say that it was one of the more solid AA experiences that I’ve had amongst the other titles mentioned above and could maybe see myself revisiting this game in the future.
